client: I've been feeling really anxious about this big presentation I have to give at our annual conference next week. Yesterday during practice, I completely blanked and forgot my lines halfway through, and now I can't stop worrying it'll happen again in front of everyone. I know you're going to suggest some techniques, but I'm not sure anything can help when my mind just goes blank like that.
therapist: It sounds like this experience with forgetting your lines has left you feeling quite nervous and doubtful about the presentation. When your mind went blank during practice, what kind of thoughts were running through your head at that moment?

client:
I just kept thinking "Everyone will see me fail" and "I'm going to embarrass myself in front of the whole team." My heart was racing so fast I could barely breathe. The worst part is I know this material - it's like my brain just shuts down when I get nervous. 

I've tried practicing more, but it doesn't seem to help because in the moment, all that preparation just disappears. I'm worried this will keep happening no matter what I do.
therapist: I hear how distressing this experience is for you, especially when you know the material well but your anxiety takes over. It might help to explore what happens if we shift from "I'm going to fail" to "I'm prepared but nervous" - would you be willing to try examining the evidence for both these thoughts?

client: I get what you're saying about reframing the thought, but when I'm in that moment of panic before a test, it's like my brain just won't listen to logic. Even if I know I'm prepared, the fear feels so real and overwhelming. It's hard to believe a different thought could make any difference.
therapist: It makes complete sense that in those intense moments, the fear feels overpowering despite knowing you're prepared. Let's try something - could you recall one small instance where you were nervous but still managed to get through it? Even something minor might help us find a starting point.

client: Hmm, I guess there was that time last week when I had to give a quick update in a team meeting. My hands were shaking but I got through it. But that feels different - it wasn't as important as the big presentation coming up, so I don't know if it really counts. The stakes feel so much higher now.
therapist: It's great that you recognized that small success in the team meeting - even though it felt different, it shows your ability to push through nervousness. What do you think made that situation feel more manageable compared to the upcoming presentation?

client: I guess it felt more manageable because the team meeting was smaller and with people I already know. But this upcoming presentation is for the whole department, and I keep imagining myself freezing up in front of all those people. Even though I got through the meeting okay, this just feels like a completely different level of pressure.
therapist: It sounds like the difference in audience size and familiarity is really amplifying your worries about this presentation. When you imagine freezing up in front of the larger group, what specific outcomes are you picturing that feel so daunting?

client: I keep picturing everyone staring at me while I stumble over my words, and then hearing people whispering or laughing afterward. It's not just about messing up - I'm terrified they'll think I'm incompetent and it'll ruin my reputation at work. Even though I've presented to my small team before, this feels completely different because it's executives I barely know.
therapist: I hear how deeply this fear of judgment is affecting you, especially with executives you don't know well. It might help to explore this: When you've seen others stumble during presentations, what was your actual impression of them afterward? Often our own fears create much harsher judgments than what others truly think.

client:
You know, when I think about it, I do remember seeing coworkers make mistakes in presentations. I didn't think less of them, but I still feel like people would judge me more harshly. There's this voice in my head saying my mistakes would be different—more noticeable or embarrassing somehow. 

It's hard to shake the feeling that I'm held to a higher standard, even though logically I know that's probably not true.
therapist: It sounds like you're recognizing this double standard where you're much more forgiving of others' mistakes than your own. That critical voice telling you "your mistakes would be worse" - when did you first notice this voice showing up in your life? Sometimes understanding its origins can help us see it more objectively.

client:
Honestly, I think that voice has been there since I was a kid. My parents were always really hard on me about grades and being perfect, while my siblings got more slack. It's just hard to believe I deserve that same kindness now. 

Even when you say that about seeing it objectively, part of me thinks "but what if they were right to be hard on me?" Like maybe I really do need that criticism to stay on track.
therapist: It sounds like these early experiences with high expectations have left you questioning whether you deserve the same compassion you easily give to others. That inner critic telling you "you need this harshness" - do you think it's actually helping you perform better, or could it be making these high-pressure situations even harder?

client: I never thought about it that way, but I guess the constant self-criticism does make everything feel more overwhelming. Whenever I make a mistake at work, that voice just makes me panic more, which makes me perform worse. But the idea of being kind to myself feels... wrong, like I'm letting myself off too easy when I should be pushing harder.
therapist: It sounds like you're beginning to notice how that harsh inner voice actually works against you, even though letting go of it feels uncomfortable. That tension between wanting to be kind to yourself and fearing you're "letting yourself off easy" - might we explore what "pushing harder" actually looks like when it's coming from encouragement rather than criticism?

client: I know logically that being kinder to myself would help, but it feels dangerous somehow. Like if I stop pushing myself so hard, I'll just become lazy and fail at everything. The criticism feels like the only thing keeping me in line sometimes.
therapist: That fear of becoming "lazy" if you're kinder to yourself sounds really unsettling - like you're walking a tightrope between self-criticism and complete failure. What if we experimented with viewing self-compassion not as letting go of standards, but as changing the fuel that drives you? For example, when you imagine preparing with encouragement rather than criticism, what specifically feels risky about that approach?
